report.title: Local-first research workspace review
report.topic: How local-first research tools handle capture, evidence, and handoff
report.scope: Desktop tools with offline storage, source traceability, and export paths suitable for an individual research workflow.
report.methodology: Two independent research lanes gathered product documentation and implementation evidence. Codex reconciled claims, checked source dates, and retained one unresolved portability question.

executive_summary: The strongest local-first tools keep the working set on the user's machine while making source identity visible beside the note or finding.
Export quality varies more than capture quality. A tool can feel excellent during research and still produce a weak handoff when links, attachments, or provenance do not survive the move.
No single option won every category. The practical choice depends on whether the user values structured evidence, flexible writing, or portable archives most.

findings.title: Local storage is common; inspectable provenance is not
findings.summary: Several tools keep notes locally, but fewer keep source identity, retrieval date, and claim linkage visible in the normal reading flow.
findings.limitations: The review covered documented behavior and a bounded desktop sample, not every plugin ecosystem.
findings.detail: Local files help with ownership and backup, but they do not automatically create a useful evidence trail. The best implementations expose source metadata without making ordinary reading feel like database administration.

findings.title: Attachment portability is the main handoff fault line
findings.summary: Markdown exports travel well until native attachments, generated files, or app-specific references are involved.
findings.limitations: Cloud-sync and mobile-only paths were outside the accepted scope.
findings.detail: A durable handoff needs both readable notes and an inventory of native files. Relative links, stable names, and hashes make that package easier to move and verify.

findings.title: Structured capture helps review but can slow first-pass work
findings.summary: Required source and confidence fields improve later review, while free-form tools remain faster during exploratory capture.
findings.limitations: The time cost depends heavily on templates and keyboard-driven capture support.
findings.detail: A useful compromise is progressive structure: capture quickly, then require evidence fields before a finding can move into the accepted set.

findings.title: Human-readable final exports need their own acceptance check
findings.summary: A structurally valid data packet can still be hard to navigate, print, or audit as a finished research deliverable.
findings.limitations: Accessibility behavior was checked on current desktop Chrome and a narrow viewport only.
findings.detail: The final reading surface should be checked against the same accepted data, then tested for navigation, keyboard use, printing, and offline behavior.

themes.name: Evidence stays attached
themes.summary: Source identity and limitations should remain close to the finding they support.

themes.name: The handoff is part of the product
themes.summary: Exports, attachments, and final reading quality determine whether research survives outside the original tool.

decisions.title: Keep native artifacts beside the accepted research packet
decisions.rationale: This preserves exact bytes while letting notes and the explorer link to one stable inventory.

recommendations.title: Use progressive evidence fields
recommendations.detail: Allow fast capture, then require sources, confidence, and limitations before a finding enters the accepted set.

recommendations.title: Test the final reading copy separately
recommendations.detail: Run keyboard, narrow-screen, offline, source-trace, and print checks against the exact accepted export.
